SUMMARY STATEMENT State of Idaho v. Scott Howard Holmes Docket No. 52430 & 52431 In these consolidated cases arising out of Twin Falls County, the Court of Appeals affirmed Scott Howard Holmes’ judgments of conviction and unified sentences for burglary, eight counts of video voyeurism, sexual exploitation of a child, and being a persistent violator of the law. In Docket No. 52430, Holmes’ ex-girlfriend reported that Holmes sent nude photographs of her to her daughter and niece. A jury found Holmes guilty of six counts of video voyeurism and he admitted to being a persistent violator. In Docket No. 52431, officers investigating Holmes discovered hidden cameras in his ex-girlfriend’s home. Officers also discovered video footage on Holmes’ cell phone of the ex-girlfriend’s fifteen-year-old daughter engaging in sexual activity. A jury found Holmes guilty of burglary, two counts of video voyeurism, and sexual exploitation of a child, and he admitted to being a persistent violator. Prior to the combined sentencing hearing, Holmes fired his attorney and, using profane language, Holmes rejected a public defender, refused to answer the district court’s questions regarding self-representation, and indicated he wanted to be removed from the courtroom. Holmes was then removed and permitted to attend the hearing virtually with his microphone turned off. On appeal, Holmes argues the district court abused its discretion by not asking him whether he would like to make a statement at the sentencing hearing. The Court disagreed and held that Holmes forfeited his procedural right to make a statement at the hearing based on his statements in the record, including his use of profanity and continued disrespectful and disruptive behavior. Holmes also asserted he did not have notice or an opportunity to be heard regarding restitution. According to Holmes, the district court abused its discretion by ordering $1,024 in restitution to his ex-girlfriend without evidence in the record supporting the amount. The Court agreed, holding it was undisputed that the record did not include evidence relating to the restitution order and that nothing in the record indicated Holmes was given notice of the restitution request, the basis of the request, or an opportunity to object. Consequently, the Court reversed the order and concluded that a remand of the case was appropriate to afford Holmes due process as it relates to restitution and a proper evidentiary record for any restitution order. This summary constitutes no part of the opinion of the Court, but has been prepared by court staff for the convenience of the public.
